blocks.title: The cell, and what kills it

cold_open.text: Four patients on one shift: a bleeding trauma, a failing heart, a severe pneumonia, and an overdose. Four different diagnoses, four different treatments, and you will not know any of the diagnoses for hours. Something is already the same about all of them.

screens.body_md:
**Almost every emergency injures a patient the same way in the end: cells not getting enough oxygen for the work they are doing.**

Hemorrhage, a failing pump, sepsis, an obstructed airway. Four causes, one destination — which is why you treat delivery before anyone can name the disease. Oxygen, ventilation, circulation and transport do not wait for a name.

**A cell short of oxygen switches to a far less efficient pathway.** It produces a fraction of the energy and accumulates acid, which is why lactate rises and why the patient starts breathing it off.

The pumps that hold its internal environment steady are the first thing it can no longer afford, and losing them is what makes the damage progressive.

**Damage accumulates while the deprivation lasts, and becomes irreversible.** Restore flow later and you restore less.

That is the physiology under every time-critical protocol you will be handed. The clock is not an administrative convention, and the window differs by tissue.

**Four points where delivery can fail.** Oxygen not reaching the blood. Not enough blood to carry it. Not enough flow to move it. Or the cell unable to use what arrives.

The last is the instructive one: cyanide poisoning presents with good saturations, good pressure, and a dying patient.

**Hypoxia is too little oxygen. Ischemia is too little flow** — and that also removes fuel and waste clearance, which is why ischemic tissue deteriorates faster for the same duration.

Saturation measures one link of four. Blood pressure measures another, badly. Two whole failure modes go unmeasured, which is why a patient with two good numbers can still be deteriorating in front of you. Knowing which link has failed is what turns four diagnoses into one plan.

blocks.callback_md:
In every one of them, cells are not getting the oxygen they need.

The bleeding patient cannot carry it. The failing heart cannot move it. The pneumonia cannot get it in. The overdose is not moving air at all.

**Four roads, one destination** — which is why your treatment is largely the same before the diagnosis arrives, and why it works. The receiving team will name it. Your job is to keep enough cells alive for the name to still matter.

blocks.title: Shock as a process

cold_open.text: Pulse 124. Skin cool and gray. Capillary refill four seconds. Anxious and asking the same question twice. Blood pressure 122 over 80, and somebody in the room says the patient is not in shock because the pressure is fine.

screens.body_md:
**Shock is inadequate perfusion of tissue for its needs.** A process, not a number.

Define it by a blood pressure and you cannot diagnose it until compensation has already failed — which is exactly too late to do anything cheap about it. Shock begins long before any number moves, and that is where you want to meet it. A pressure is a late confirmation of something you could already see.

**Three stages.** Compensated: perfusion maintained by a faster heart and constricted vessels, with the pressure still normal. Decompensated: compensation fails and the pressure falls. Irreversible: cellular damage beyond recovery even if flow returns.

Only the first is reliably reversible by anything you do.

**Four findings, none of which needs a monitor.** Tachycardia at rest. Cool, pale or mottled skin. Delayed capillary refill. Anxiety or restlessness as cerebral perfusion falls.

Those are what you are looking for. Hypotension is what most people wait for, and waiting costs a stage — the only one that reliably responds to anything you carry.

**Capillary refill deserves an honest note.** It is affected by ambient temperature, age and lighting, and assessors agree imperfectly — better in children than adults.

Worth doing, worth recording, not worth a decision on its own. A cold patient on a cold night refills slowly for reasons that are not shock, and a warm septic patient may refill briskly while dying.

**Children are the extreme case.** They compensate extremely well and then decompensate abruptly, with very little warning in the numbers.

Chapter 9 spent a whole block on a heart rate that fell into the normal range. This is why: in a child the numbers look reassuring right up until they do not. Treat the four findings, and treat them before the cuff agrees with you.

blocks.callback_md:
You are. That patient is in compensated shock, and the normal pressure is the compensation succeeding rather than evidence against it.

Four findings point one way and one number has not moved yet. **The pressure is the last thing to go**, which makes it the last thing to trust — and by the time it falls you have lost the stage that was cheap to treat.

blocks.title: Categories of shock
blocks.learner_title: Which one, and does fluid help?

cold_open.text: Two patients in shock. One has flat neck veins and clear lungs. The other has distended neck veins and crackles throughout. They will get very different treatment, and the two findings that separated them cost nothing and took four seconds.
cold_open.decision_point: What did those two findings tell you?

screens.body_md:
**Four categories.** Hypovolemic — the container has emptied. Cardiogenic — the pump has failed. Distributive — the container has dilated. Obstructive — filling or outflow is physically blocked.

The category decides the treatment, and you can decide it at the bedside, in the first minute, without naming the disease at all. None of the four requires a diagnosis to identify.

**Two free findings separate most of them.** The neck veins and the lungs.

Flat veins and clear lungs: an empty container. Distended veins with wet lungs: a failed pump. Distended veins with clear lungs: something obstructing filling. Warm skin and bounding pulses: a dilated one. Four patterns, two observations, and no equipment. Look at both before you look at anything else.

**Distributive shock is the one that does not look like shock.** Anaphylaxis, sepsis and high spinal injury all dilate the vessels, so the skin can be warm and flushed with a normal capillary refill.

In cord injury the heart rate often fails to rise at all, because the injury disconnected the compensation.

**Fluid is not a general treatment for shock.** It helps an empty container. It worsens pulmonary edema in a failed pump. It achieves very little against a mechanical obstruction, where the answer is a procedure.

So the category is not an academic exercise. It decides whether your intervention helps or harms, and there is no neutral option once fluid is running.

**A patient can be in two categories at once**, and trauma is where that happens: hemorrhage and a tension pneumothorax together.

If your intervention was right for the category and nothing improved, either the category was wrong or there is a second one. Reassess after every intervention, and treat no improvement as information rather than as bad luck. Category first, then the name, then the reassessment that checks you were right.

blocks.callback_md:
Flat veins and clear lungs: an empty container, and fluid is the answer.

Distended veins and wet lungs: a failed pump, with pressure backing up behind it — and fluid makes that patient worse.

**Same presenting problem, opposite treatment, and the two findings that decided it needed no equipment at all.** That is the case for categorizing before you can name anything.

blocks.title: Compensation and its failure

cold_open.text: A bleeding patient’s heart rate has been 140 for twenty minutes. Over the next four it comes down to 60, and the blood pressure has not changed. Your partner says the fluid must be working.

screens.body_md:
**Compensation preserves the brain and heart by sacrificing everywhere else.** Skin, gut and kidney are given up first, deliberately.

So every compensation finding is a cost being paid somewhere. Cold skin is the price of a warm brain, and falling urine output is the price of both. Read each finding as a cost, and you can tell how hard the body is working. Nothing here is repair; all of it is borrowing against time.

**Four mechanisms.** Heart rate up — fastest and first. Peripheral vessels constricted — the cool, pale skin. Respiratory rate up, blowing off accumulating acid. And fluid retained through the kidneys, which is slower.

Three of the four are visible within seconds of walking in, before you have touched anyone or opened a bag. Each one costs the patient something, and each one is finite.

**A rising respiratory rate is a circulatory finding.** A patient breathing fast with clear lungs and no distress is frequently telling you about their perfusion rather than their chest.

It is one of the earliest signs of shock and one of the most consistently written off as anxiety.

**Some patients cannot compensate.** Older adults have a blunted baroreceptor response, and a beta blocker removes the heart rate rise entirely.

A patient on a beta blocker can be in significant shock at a rate of 70. The absence of tachycardia is not the absence of shock.

**And compensation runs out.** A heart rate falling in a bleeding patient is not improvement — it is the mechanism exhausted, and it is a pre-arrest finding.

Chapter 9 made the same point about an infant. A number moving into the normal range is only good news if something made it better. Ask what changed before you believe a number that has improved on its own.

blocks.callback_md:
No. Nothing has improved — the compensation has failed.

The rate came down because the mechanism ran out, not because the bleeding stopped, and the unchanged pressure is about to stop being unchanged. **This is a pre-arrest finding wearing the appearance of a normal number.**

If an intervention worked you would expect the skin, the mental state and the pressure to move with it. Nothing else moved, so nothing else improved.

blocks.title: Respiratory failure

cold_open.text: A breathless patient has been loud, frightened and working hard for twenty minutes. Now she is quiet, her rate has slowed, and she is easier to be in the room with. Somebody says the treatment is working.

screens.body_md:
**Three ways the system fails.** Ventilation — air not moving. Diffusion — gas not crossing the membrane. Matching — air and blood not arriving in the same place.

A pulmonary embolism is the clearest matching failure: the lung is ventilated perfectly and there is no blood there to collect the oxygen, and no amount of extra oxygen reaches a capillary that nothing is flowing through. Deciding which one is the first move on any breathless patient.

**Which failure you are watching decides what helps.** Oxygen works best on a gradient problem and worst on a shunt, where blood bypasses ventilated lung entirely.

So a hypoxic patient who barely improves on oxygen is telling you something specific about the mechanism, not about the equipment.

**Watch the work, not the number.** Accessory muscle use and retractions. Inability to speak in full sentences. A climbing rate with falling depth.

A patient on oxygen can hold a normal saturation while heading toward respiratory arrest. The saturation is a supporting finding; the effort is the finding, and it is visible from the end of the bed.

**Carbon dioxide clearance depends almost entirely on minute volume.** So a patient not moving air accumulates it quickly — and rising carbon dioxide is itself sedating.

Which is why a tiring patient becomes drowsy and then stops, rather than fighting to the end. Exhaustion looks like calm, and it is the single most misread transition in respiratory emergencies.

**Quiet is the dangerous sign.** A silent chest in asthma is worse than a wheezing one. A slowing rate in an exhausted patient is worse than a fast one.

And all of it leads back to 8.1: this is one route to the same endpoint, cells not getting the oxygen they need. Air, membrane, matching — three doors into the same room.

blocks.callback_md:
No. She is exhausted, and her carbon dioxide is climbing and sedating her.

Quiet, drowsy and slowing after twenty minutes of hard work is not settling — it is the transition to respiratory arrest, and it is routinely misread as improvement because the room becomes calmer.

**Loud and working hard is frightening. Quiet and drowsy is worse.** Check the effort, the speech and the depth, and be ready to breathe for her.

blocks.title: Fluid, electrolytes and acid-base

cold_open.text: A patient is breathing 28 times a minute. Their chest is completely clear, their saturation is 98 per cent on room air, and they do not look distressed by it at all. Two crews have now recorded it as respiratory distress.

screens.body_md:
**This block is context tier**: it explains findings you will meet, and very little of it changes an AEMT action by itself.

The same filter as 7.8. Read it once, use it to make sense of a pattern, and do not expect it in the review queue competing with material that changes what your hands do. It is here to explain a pattern, not to be memorized.

**The one sentence worth carrying**: a raised respiratory rate with a clear chest and no distress is often a circulatory or metabolic finding rather than a respiratory one.

The patient is blowing off acid produced by tissue that is not being perfused. The lungs are fine and are being used to correct something else.

**Fluid leaves the circulation in more ways than bleeding.** Vomiting and diarrhea over days. Sweating. And fluid shifting out of the vessels into tissue, as in sepsis and burns — where total body water may be normal while the circulation is empty.

Electrolytes go with the water, which is why replacing water alone is not the whole answer.

**Potassium is the electrolyte that matters most to you**, because it affects rhythm and because the at-risk patients are identifiable from the history: renal failure, crush injury, a missed dialysis session.

You will not measure it. You can predict who has it, which is the useful form of the knowledge — a history that raises your index of suspicion before any rhythm appears.

**Do not suppress a compensation you have not understood.** The fast breathing in a shocked or ketoacidotic patient is fixing something.

Removing it — by over-sedating, for instance — takes away the correction and leaves the cause, and the patient gets worse in a way that looks like a drug effect. Understand the compensation before you interfere with it.

blocks.callback_md:
Almost certainly not.

Clear chest, normal saturation, no distress, and a rate of 28. That combination points at perfusion or metabolism, and the breathing is the compensation rather than the problem.

**Recording it as respiratory distress sends the next clinician to the lungs**, which is where there is nothing to find — and it is why this short, context-tier block earns its place.

blocks.title: Inflammation, immunity and sepsis
blocks.learner_title: The one your screen will miss

cold_open.text: An 80-year-old, confused since yesterday, breathing at 26 with a clear chest, warm dry skin, and a temperature of 35.6 degrees. No fever. Your service’s sepsis screening tool comes back negative, and everyone in the room relaxes slightly.

evidence_flag.textbook_position: qSOFA — altered mentation, respiratory rate 22 or more, systolic pressure 100 or less — is widely taught as the quick bedside screen for sepsis, and is built into many prehospital screening tools as the single trigger.
evidence_flag.current_evidence: The 2021 Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines make a **strong recommendation, on moderate quality evidence, against using qSOFA as a single screening tool**, on the grounds of **low sensitivity** — it is more specific and less sensitive than two of four SIRS criteria for identifying infection-induced organ dysfunction. The guidelines point instead to using SIRS, NEWS or MEWS alongside clinical judgment and lactate where available.
evidence_flag.uncertainty: What this does not mean is that qSOFA is useless or that any alternative is good. No prehospital sepsis screen has the sensitivity to rule sepsis out, and the alternatives named perform better in that one respect rather than well in general. The operational conclusion is narrow and firm: a negative screen never overrides a clinical suspicion, and a screen that is specific and insensitive will let sick patients through by design.
evidence_flag.source_ref: Evans L et al., Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021, Crit Care Med 2021;49(11):e1063 · Singer M et al., Sepsis-3, JAMA 2016;315:801

screens.body_md:
**Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection.**

The response, not the organism, does the damage — which is why the definition moved onto organ dysfunction in 2016, and why bacteria in the blood is neither necessary nor sufficient. Sepsis can outrun the infection that started it. That is why it can arrive without a fever and without a positive screen.

**Inflammation is normally local and useful**: increased flow and vessel permeability bringing immune cells to a site. Redness, warmth, swelling, pain.

Sepsis is that process going system-wide. Vessels dilate and leak everywhere at once, which is the distributive shock of 8.3 arriving by a different route.

**So the septic patient can be warm.** Warm skin, a full pulse, a normal capillary refill — and failing perfusion at the tissue underneath all of it.

Every other block taught cool and pale as the shock skin. This is the one that is warm, and it is the one most often sent home.

**Four findings, no equipment.** New confusion or any change in mental status. A raised respiratory rate. Tachycardia with warm skin. And a temperature that is high *or low* — hypothermia in infection is a bad sign, not a reassuring one.

Older patients frequently present with no fever at all, and with no raised white count when somebody finally measures one.

**Your contribution is recognition and speed.** Identify it, alert the receiving hospital, and move — time to treatment drives outcome, and the treatments are theirs rather than yours.

Which is exactly why the screening question in the panel before this one matters so much at this level: the recognition is the whole of your contribution. Recognize, alert, move, and say what your screen did and did not show.

blocks.callback_md:
No.

New confusion against a known baseline, a respiratory rate of 26 with a clear chest, warm skin in a patient who is not perfusing, and a temperature of 35.6 — **the absence of fever makes this worse, not better.** That is four findings pointing at sepsis, and a screen with known low sensitivity saying no.

Alert on your suspicion, and say the screen was negative and why you are alerting anyway. Both halves belong in the handover.

blocks.title: Risk that arrives with the patient

cold_open.text: Two patients, identical findings: a minor head strike, fully alert, a normal neurological examination and no other injury. One takes an anticoagulant. Everything about the next six hours is different for that one, and nothing you can examine will tell you which is which.
cold_open.decision_point: What is the history actually worth?

screens.body_md:
**A history is a prior, not a list to transcribe.** It shifts the probabilities before you have examined anyone, and it changes what a normal finding is worth.

Diabetes, dialysis, immunosuppression, anticoagulation. Each one makes some things likelier and some reassurances less reliable. Asking properly takes fifteen seconds and reshapes the assessment that follows. It also decides how much a normal number is allowed to reassure you.

**Four histories that change an ordinary finding.** Anticoagulation after any head strike — a minor mechanism becomes significant, and a normal examination now says less about the next six hours.

Immunosuppression with infection. A missed dialysis session. Diabetes with atypical or absent chest pain.

**Medications change the numbers you are reading.** A beta blocker removes the tachycardia you are looking for. Treated hypertension means a "normal" pressure may be low for that person.

Know the patient before you read the monitor. That phrase is doing real work here.

**Genetic susceptibility plus exposure over time is how most common disease arrives.** Rarely one alone.

So a family history of early cardiac death in a middle-aged patient with chest pain is not a diagnosis. It is a reason to take the presentation more seriously, not less.

**And the risk of all this is anchoring**: attributing new findings to the familiar condition and missing something else. The frequent caller with a new problem is the classic case, and chapter 1 met them from the other side.

Use the history to decide where to look. Then examine the patient as though you did not know any of it, and let the findings argue back. The history tells you where to look; it never tells you what is there.

blocks.callback_md:
It is worth the thing your examination cannot give you: what happens next.

Both patients are fine now. One has a meaningfully higher risk of delayed intracranial bleeding, and no finding at the scene will separate them — **the history is the only instrument that can**.

That is the case for asking properly. And it is also the warning: the same history, used lazily, is how a new problem gets filed under an old diagnosis.

blocks.title: Integration — a screen that said no

cold_open.text: The call that tests this chapter is not the dramatic one. It is an older person who is not herself, with numbers that individually look survivable, a medication list that changes what two of them mean, and a screening tool that returns a negative and invites everyone to stop thinking.

screens.body_md:
**Five questions, and the tool answers none of them.**

Which link of the delivery chain is failing? Which category of shock, and which stage? What is compensation doing, and what is it being blocked by? What does the history change about the numbers? And what does a negative screen actually establish?

What follows is one call. Everything in this chapter is in it.

blocks.callback_md:
Yes, and it takes about ninety seconds.

Confusion against a lucid Friday. A rate of 26 with a clear chest — compensation, not a lung problem. A temperature of 35.7 in a suspected infection, which is worse than a fever. Warm skin with a full pulse: a dilated container. A pulse of 112 **on a beta blocker**, meaning more than the number says. And no urine since yesterday, which is a fourth organ agreeing.

**Six findings, one negative screen, and the screen is the thing that was wrong.** Knowing why is the whole chapter.

items.stem: Select the findings that suggest compensated shock.

options.rationale: The cheapest compensation available and usually the first.

items.stem: Why is hypotension a poor early screen for shock?

options.text: Compensation holds the pressure up until a large proportion of reserve is gone, especially in the young
options.rationale: By the time it falls, you are in the second stage.

options.text: Blood pressure cannot be measured accurately prehospital
options.rationale: It usually can.

options.text: Blood pressure is unrelated to perfusion
options.rationale: It is related and it is a lagging indicator.

options.text: Only trauma patients develop hypotension
options.rationale: Not so.

items.explanation_md: A pressure that has finally fallen in a young patient is not the beginning of a problem. It is the failure of a compensation that has been working hard for some time.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

items.stem: How reliable is capillary refill as a perfusion measure in an adult?

options.text: Useful as one finding among several — it is affected by ambient temperature, age and lighting, and agreement between assessors is imperfect
options.rationale: Better in children than adults, and never on its own.

options.text: A definitive measure of perfusion in all patients
options.rationale: It is not definitive in anyone.

options.text: Of no value at any age
options.rationale: It is useful, particularly in children.

options.text: Reliable only when measured with a monitor
options.rationale: It is a bedside observation.

items.explanation_md: Worth doing, worth recording, and not worth hanging a decision on alone. A cold patient on a cold night refills slowly for reasons that are not shock.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

items.stem: Which stage does this describe?

rows.label: Pulse 124, cool peripheries, blood pressure 122/80, anxious
Pulse 136, weak radial pulse, blood pressure 78/40, drowsy
Pulse 110, pale, alert, pressure normal for the patient
Bradycardia and hypotension in a bleeding patient

items.explanation_md: The last row is the worst. A falling heart rate in a bleeding patient is not improvement — it is compensation exhausted, and it is a pre-arrest finding.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

items.stem: Why is shock in a child particularly dangerous to assess?

options.text: Children compensate extremely well and then decompensate abruptly, with little warning in the numbers
options.rationale: The cliff edge is steep and it arrives late.

options.text: Children do not develop shock
options.rationale: They do.

options.text: Children show hypotension earliest
options.rationale: They show it latest.

options.text: Vital signs cannot be measured in children
options.rationale: They can, and the ranges are in chapter 9.

items.explanation_md: Which is why chapter 9 spent a whole block on a heart rate that fell into the normal range. In a child the numbers look reassuring until they do not.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

items.stem: What does treating shock as a process rather than a number change about what you do?

options.text: You act on the findings of compensation instead of waiting for a pressure to confirm them
options.rationale: Oxygen, position, warmth, transport, and a destination that can fix the cause.

options.text: You stop measuring blood pressure
options.rationale: You measure it and you do not wait for it.

options.text: You delay transport until the stage is confirmed
options.rationale: The opposite.

options.text: Nothing changes operationally
options.rationale: It changes when you start.

items.explanation_md: The entire value of this block is the minutes it buys, and those minutes come from acting on four bedside findings rather than one cuff reading.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

items.stem: Sort each cause into its category of shock.

options.text: Major hemorrhage or severe dehydration
options.rationale: Volume lost from the container.

options.text: Large myocardial infarction with poor output
options.rationale: The pump has failed.

options.text: Anaphylaxis, sepsis or high spinal injury
options.rationale: The container has dilated.

options.text: Tension pneumothorax or cardiac tamponade
options.rationale: Filling or outflow physically obstructed.

items.explanation_md: Four categories, and the category decides the treatment. Fluid helps an empty container and can drown a failed pump.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

items.stem: Why does the category of shock matter more than the diagnosis prehospital?

options.text: It determines whether fluid, position and oxygen help or harm, and you can determine it at the bedside
options.rationale: You can categorize without naming the disease.

options.text: It determines the destination only
options.rationale: It does that too, and the treatment change is larger.

options.text: It is needed for documentation
options.rationale: Not the reason.

options.text: It does not — treatment is the same in all shock
options.rationale: Treatment differs substantially between categories.

items.explanation_md: Fluid into a failed pump worsens pulmonary edema. Fluid into an obstructed circulation does very little. Category first, name later.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

items.stem: A patient in shock has distended neck veins and crackles throughout both lungs. Which category is most likely?

options.text: Cardiogenic — the pump has failed and pressure is backing up behind it
options.rationale: Full veins and wet lungs point away from an empty container.

options.text: Hypovolemic
options.rationale: Neck veins would be flat and lungs clear.

options.text: Distributive
options.rationale: Usually warm peripheries and no pulmonary edema early.

options.text: Obstructive
options.rationale: Neck veins may be distended, and diffuse crackles fit the pump better.

items.explanation_md: Two free findings — the neck and the chest — separate the commonest categories without any equipment at all.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

items.stem: Is fluid likely to help this patient?

rows.label: Hemorrhage from a femoral wound, controlled
Pulmonary edema with a failing left ventricle
Severe dehydration from three days of vomiting
Tension pneumothorax, before decompression

items.explanation_md: Two empty containers and two problems fluid cannot reach. The tension needs the pressure released; the failing ventricle needs less volume, not more.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

items.stem: Why can a patient in distributive shock have warm, flushed skin?

options.text: The vessels are dilated rather than constricted — the container has enlarged instead of emptying
options.rationale: Which is why the classic cool, pale picture can be absent.

options.text: They are febrile only
options.rationale: Fever may be present; dilation is the mechanism.

options.text: Their perfusion is adequate
options.rationale: Perfusion is failing despite the warmth.

options.text: It is a sign of early recovery
options.rationale: It is not.

items.explanation_md: This is the shock that does not look like shock. Warm skin and a normal capillary refill do not exclude it, particularly in sepsis.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

items.stem: A high spinal cord injury produces shock. Which category, and why?

options.text: Distributive — sympathetic control of vessel tone is lost, so the vessels dilate
options.rationale: Often with a heart rate that fails to rise, which is the giveaway.

options.text: Hypovolemic, from bleeding at the injury site
options.rationale: Cord injury itself does not cause that volume loss.

options.text: Cardiogenic, from direct cardiac injury
options.rationale: The heart is structurally intact.

options.text: Obstructive
options.rationale: Nothing is obstructing filling or outflow.

items.explanation_md: Hypotension without tachycardia in a patient with a cord injury is the pattern. The compensation you would expect is exactly what the injury has disconnected.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

items.stem: Select the findings that point toward obstructive shock.

options.text: Distended neck veins with clear lung fields
options.rationale: Filling is obstructed, not the lungs flooded.

options.text: Unequal or absent breath sounds on one side
options.rationale: Tension pneumothorax.

options.text: Tracheal deviation away from the affected side, when present
options.rationale: A late sign, and highly suggestive when it appears.

options.text: Shock that does not respond to fluid
options.rationale: Because the problem is mechanical.

options.text: Warm, flushed skin with bounding pulses
options.rationale: That points toward distributive shock.

items.explanation_md: Obstructive shock is the category where the answer is a procedure rather than a fluid. Recognizing it is what gets that procedure requested.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

items.stem: A patient can be in more than one category at once. Why does that matter?

options.text: Treating only the category you recognized first can leave the other untreated and the patient unimproved
options.rationale: Trauma with both hemorrhage and a tension is the common example.

options.text: It does not happen
options.rationale: It happens regularly.

options.text: It means categorizing is pointless
options.rationale: It means reassessing after each intervention.

options.text: It only occurs in medical patients
options.rationale: It is most common in trauma.

items.explanation_md: If your intervention was right for the category and nothing improved, either the category was wrong or there is a second one.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

items.stem: What is compensation actually doing?

options.text: Preserving perfusion to the brain and heart by sacrificing everywhere else
options.rationale: Skin, gut and kidney are given up first, deliberately.

options.text: Repairing the underlying injury
options.rationale: It buys time; it repairs nothing.

options.text: Reducing the body’s oxygen requirement
options.rationale: Demand often rises.

options.text: Restoring lost volume
options.rationale: It redistributes what is left.

items.explanation_md: Every compensation finding is a cost being paid somewhere. Cold skin is the price of a warm brain.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

items.stem: Select the mechanisms the body uses to compensate for falling perfusion.

options.text: Increasing heart rate
options.rationale: Fastest and cheapest, and the first to appear.

options.text: Constricting peripheral vessels
options.rationale: Which produces the cool, pale skin.

options.text: Increasing respiratory rate to blow off acid
options.rationale: Respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis.

options.text: Retaining fluid through the kidneys
options.rationale: Slower, and it is why urine output falls.

options.text: Lowering body temperature deliberately
options.rationale: Hypothermia in shock is a consequence, not a compensation.

items.explanation_md: Four mechanisms, and three of them are visible at the bedside within seconds. The fourth is why you ask about urine output.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

items.stem: A bleeding patient’s heart rate falls from 140 to 60 and the pressure is unchanged. How do you read that?

options.text: Compensation has failed — this is a pre-arrest finding, not an improvement
options.rationale: The rate fell because the mechanism ran out, not because the problem resolved.

options.text: The bleeding has stopped
options.rationale: Nothing here suggests that.

options.text: A normal response to analgesia
options.rationale: Not across that range in a bleeding patient.

options.text: Improvement — the rate is now normal
options.rationale: The most dangerous misreading in this chapter.

items.explanation_md: Chapter 9 made the same point about an infant. A number moving into the normal range is only good news if something made it better.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

items.stem: Why do older adults and patients on certain medications compensate poorly?

options.text: Blunted baroreceptor response and drugs that block the heart rate rise remove the main compensation
options.rationale: Beta blockade in particular can hide the tachycardia you are looking for.

options.text: They have less blood volume
options.rationale: Not the primary mechanism.

options.text: They feel less pain
options.rationale: Unrelated to compensation.

options.text: They do not develop shock
options.rationale: They develop it and show it later.

items.explanation_md: A patient on a beta blocker can be in significant shock with a heart rate of 70. The absence of tachycardia is not the absence of shock.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

items.stem: Is compensation working, failing, or absent?

rows.label: Pulse 126, cool skin, normal pressure
Pulse 58 and falling in a bleeding patient
Hypotensive with a pulse of 72 on a beta blocker
Hypotensive, drowsy, pulse 140 and thready

items.explanation_md: Three different readings of a heart rate, and the number alone tells you none of them. The context is the whole finding.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

items.stem: Why is a rising respiratory rate a circulatory finding as well as a respiratory one?

options.text: Acid accumulating from anaerobic metabolism is blown off by breathing faster
options.rationale: Respiratory compensation for a metabolic problem.

options.text: It always indicates lung disease
options.rationale: It frequently indicates a perfusion problem.

options.text: It indicates anxiety only
options.rationale: Anxiety is a differential, not the explanation to settle on.

options.text: It has no circulatory meaning
options.rationale: It is one of the earliest signs of shock.

items.explanation_md: A patient breathing fast with clear lungs and no distress is often telling you about their circulation. It is one of the most overlooked findings there is.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

items.stem: What does falling urine output indicate in a patient who is otherwise compensating?

options.text: Blood is being diverted away from the kidneys — a compensation cost, and an early organ effect
options.rationale: It is a slower marker and a real one.

options.text: Dehydration only
options.rationale: It occurs with normal hydration when perfusion falls.

options.text: Kidney disease
options.rationale: Possible, and not the first reading in a shocked patient.

options.text: Nothing relevant prehospital
options.rationale: It is worth asking about, particularly in the elderly.

items.explanation_md: You rarely measure it on an ambulance, and you can ask. "When did you last pass urine?" is a perfusion question wearing ordinary clothes.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

items.stem: What is the practical use of knowing how compensation works?

options.text: It tells you how much reserve is left, and therefore how quickly this patient can change
options.rationale: A patient compensating hard is closer to the edge than the numbers suggest.

options.text: It allows you to predict the diagnosis
options.rationale: It does not.

options.text: It replaces serial observations
options.rationale: It is the reason for them.

options.text: It determines drug dosing
options.rationale: Not at this level.

items.explanation_md: Reserve is the thing you are actually estimating on every unwell patient, and it is what decides how far away a hospital is allowed to be.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

items.stem: What are the three ways the respiratory system fails?

options.text: Not moving air, not getting gas across the membrane, or air and blood not meeting in the same place
options.rationale: Ventilation, diffusion, and matching.

options.text: Only by airway obstruction
options.rationale: One cause of one of the three.

options.text: Only by lung disease
options.rationale: Many failures involve healthy lungs.

options.text: By low oxygen in the air alone
options.rationale: A rare environmental cause.

items.explanation_md: Ventilation, diffusion, matching. Three failure modes, and the treatment differs between them — which is why it is worth deciding which one you are watching.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

items.stem: Which failure does this describe?

rows.label: Opioid overdose, rate 4, good volumes when breaths occur
Pulmonary edema with fluid across the membrane
Pulmonary embolism — ventilated lung with no blood reaching it
Chest wall injury with shallow splinted breathing

items.explanation_md: The embolism is the instructive one: the lung is working, the air is arriving, and there is no blood there to collect it.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

items.stem: A patient is hypoxic and supplemental oxygen barely helps. What does that suggest?

options.text: A matching or shunt problem — blood is passing lung that is not being ventilated at all
options.rationale: Raising the oxygen in ventilated alveoli does not help blood that never meets them.

options.text: The oxygen is not being delivered properly
options.rationale: Check it, and the physiology explains it better.

options.text: The patient is not trying
options.rationale: Not a mechanism.

options.text: The saturation probe is faulty
options.rationale: Worth confirming and rarely the answer.

items.explanation_md: Oxygen helps most when the problem is a gradient or low inspired concentration. It helps least when blood bypasses ventilated lung entirely.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

items.stem: Select the signs that a patient’s work of breathing is unsustainable.

options.text: Accessory muscle use and retractions
options.rationale: Work being done that the diaphragm alone cannot manage.

options.text: Inability to speak in full sentences
options.rationale: A simple, sensitive measure of reserve.

options.text: A rising respiratory rate with falling tidal volume
options.rationale: Rate climbing as depth fails.

options.text: Exhaustion, drowsiness or a falling respiratory rate late on
options.rationale: The most ominous of the four.

options.text: A normal oxygen saturation
options.rationale: It can be normal until very late, particularly on oxygen.

items.explanation_md: The last one is the trap. A patient on oxygen can maintain saturation while heading toward respiratory arrest, and the work of breathing is what tells you.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

items.stem: A breathless patient becomes quiet and drowsy with a slowing respiratory rate. What is happening?

options.text: Exhaustion and rising carbon dioxide — this is imminent respiratory arrest, not settling
options.rationale: The quiet chest is the dangerous chest.

options.text: The bronchospasm is resolving
options.rationale: A silent chest in asthma is worse, not better.

options.text: The patient is more comfortable
options.rationale: They are running out.

options.text: The oxygen is working
options.rationale: Falling rate with drowsiness is not a response to oxygen.

items.explanation_md: Loud and working hard is frightening. Quiet and drowsy is worse, and it is the transition that gets misread as improvement.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

items.stem: Why does carbon dioxide rise in a patient who is not moving enough air?

options.text: Clearance depends almost entirely on minute volume, so reduced movement accumulates it quickly
options.rationale: It diffuses readily; what limits it is how much air moves.

options.text: Because oxygen displaces it
options.rationale: Not the mechanism.

options.text: Because production increases
options.rationale: Production is roughly constant.

options.text: It does not rise in ventilatory failure
options.rationale: It is the defining feature of it.

items.explanation_md: And rising carbon dioxide is itself sedating, which is why a tiring patient becomes drowsy and then stops breathing rather than fighting to the end.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

items.stem: Why can a patient in respiratory failure have a normal oxygen saturation?

options.text: Supplemental oxygen can maintain saturation while ventilation fails and carbon dioxide climbs
options.rationale: Saturation measures one thing, and not the one that is failing.

options.text: Saturation is unaffected by respiratory failure
options.rationale: It is affected — eventually.

options.text: The probe reads arterial pressure
options.rationale: It does not.

options.text: Only children show this pattern
options.rationale: It occurs at any age.

items.explanation_md: This is why the assessment is the chest, the speech and the effort, and the number on the screen is a supporting finding rather than the finding.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

items.stem: What links respiratory failure back to the rest of this chapter?

options.text: It is one route to the same endpoint — cells not getting the oxygen they need
options.rationale: Different entry point, identical destination.

options.text: Nothing — it is a separate system
options.rationale: It is the first half of the delivery chain.

options.text: It only matters in isolation
options.rationale: It rarely occurs in isolation for long.

options.text: It is unrelated to perfusion
options.rationale: Delivery is ventilation and perfusion together.

items.explanation_md: Air in, blood around, cells fed. Failure anywhere on that chain produces the same tired, confused, deteriorating patient, and the assessment is what locates it.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

items.stem: Why is this block marked as context rather than core?

options.text: It explains findings you will meet, and very little of it changes an AEMT action on its own
options.rationale: Useful for understanding; not a spaced-repetition target.

options.text: Because it is unimportant
options.rationale: It explains a great deal of what you will see.

options.text: Because it belongs to paramedic practice
options.rationale: It is relevant at this level as understanding.

options.text: Because it is covered in chapter 7
options.rationale: Chapter 7 set up the framework; this applies it.

items.explanation_md: The same filter as 7.8. If it will not change what your hands do, it is here to make sense of findings rather than to be drilled.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

items.stem: Why does a patient in shock breathe fast even with clear lungs?

options.text: They are blowing off acid produced by anaerobic metabolism — respiratory compensation for a metabolic problem
options.rationale: The lungs are fine; they are being used to correct something else.

options.text: Because they are anxious
options.rationale: Anxiety may be present and is not the mechanism.

options.text: Because oxygen levels are always low in shock
options.rationale: Saturation can be entirely normal.

options.text: Because of airway obstruction
options.rationale: Not indicated by clear lungs.

items.explanation_md: Kussmaul breathing in diabetic ketoacidosis is the same mechanism, more obviously. Fast, deep and clear-chested is a metabolic sign.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

items.stem: Select what fluid loss from the body can look like prehospital.

options.text: Vomiting and diarrhea over days
options.rationale: Slow, large, and frequently underestimated.

options.text: Hemorrhage, external or internal
options.rationale: The fastest route.

options.text: Excessive sweating in heat or exertion
options.rationale: With electrolyte loss alongside.

options.text: Fluid shifting out of the circulation into tissue, as in sepsis or burns
options.rationale: Total body water may be normal while the circulation is empty.

options.text: Increased urine output alone in a healthy person
options.rationale: Normal regulation, not a loss state.

items.explanation_md: The fourth is the one that catches people out: a septic or burned patient can be profoundly underfilled without having lost a drop from the body.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

items.stem: What is the practical significance of potassium disturbance at this level?

options.text: It affects cardiac rhythm, and the patients at risk — renal failure, crush injury, missed dialysis — can be identified from the history
options.rationale: You will not measure it; you can predict who has it.

options.text: It affects the respiratory rate primarily
options.rationale: Cardiac effects dominate.

options.text: It has no prehospital relevance
options.rationale: It explains arrhythmia in identifiable patients.

options.text: It can be measured with a glucometer
options.rationale: It cannot.

items.explanation_md: A missed dialysis session is a rhythm risk. That is the useful form of this knowledge: a history that raises your index of suspicion.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

items.stem: Acid building up, or being blown off?

rows.label: Prolonged shock with anaerobic metabolism
Deep rapid breathing in diabetic ketoacidosis
Respiratory arrest with no ventilation
Raised respiratory rate in a compensating shocked patient

items.explanation_md: Two rows are the problem and two are the response to it. Suppressing the response — for instance by over-sedating — removes the compensation and not the cause.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

items.stem: Why does understanding acid-base change how you interpret a respiratory rate?

options.text: A fast rate may be fixing a metabolic problem rather than signaling a lung one
options.rationale: Treating it as respiratory distress can send you looking in the wrong place.

options.text: It means the rate is unimportant
options.rationale: It makes it more informative, not less.

options.text: It applies only to diabetic patients
options.rationale: It applies to any metabolic acidosis, shock included.

options.text: It changes the normal ranges
options.rationale: The ranges are unchanged.

items.explanation_md: Clear chest, no distress, high rate. That combination should turn your attention to perfusion and metabolism rather than to the lungs.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

items.stem: A patient has lost fluid over three days of vomiting. What else have they lost?

options.text: Electrolytes alongside the water, which is why replacing water alone is not the whole answer
options.rationale: Sodium, potassium and chloride go with it.

options.text: Only water
options.rationale: Gastrointestinal losses are rich in electrolytes.

options.text: Only potassium
options.rationale: Several are lost together.

options.text: Nothing measurable
options.rationale: The losses are substantial over days.

items.explanation_md: Which is why these patients get a balanced fluid rather than plain water, and why they can be arrhythmic as well as dry.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

items.stem: What is the single most useful thing from this block at the bedside?

options.text: That a raised respiratory rate with a clear chest is often a circulatory or metabolic finding
options.rationale: It redirects the assessment in the right direction.

options.text: The precise normal serum potassium range
options.rationale: You will not measure it.

options.text: The bicarbonate buffer equation
options.rationale: Not actionable prehospital.

options.text: The names of the acid-base disorders
options.rationale: Naming them changes nothing you do.

items.explanation_md: One transferable sentence out of a large subject. That is why the block is context tier and why it is short.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

items.stem: How is sepsis currently defined?

options.text: Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection
options.rationale: The response, not the organism, is what does the damage.

options.text: Any infection with a fever
options.rationale: Most infections with fever are not sepsis.

options.text: Bacteria present in the bloodstream
options.rationale: That is bacteremia, which is neither necessary nor sufficient.

options.text: Infection with a systolic pressure below 90
options.rationale: That is closer to septic shock, and it is a late definition.

items.explanation_md: The 2016 consensus moved the definition onto organ dysfunction. It is the patient’s own response that injures them, which is why sepsis can outrun the infection.
items.source_ref: Singer M, Deutschman CS, Seymour CW, et al. The Third International Consensus Definitions for Sepsis and Septic Shock (Sepsis-3). JAMA 2016;315:801–10.

items.stem: What do current sepsis guidelines say about using qSOFA as a screening tool?

options.text: They recommend strongly against using it as a single screening tool, because it misses too many patients
options.rationale: A strong recommendation on moderate quality evidence, on the grounds of low sensitivity.

options.text: They recommend it as the preferred single screen
options.rationale: That is the practice the 2021 guidelines moved away from.

options.text: They take no position on it
options.rationale: The position is explicit and strong.

options.text: They recommend it only in children
options.rationale: Not the recommendation.

items.explanation_md: qSOFA is specific and insensitive. It identifies sick patients well and it lets sick patients through, which is the wrong failure mode for a screen.
items.source_ref: Evans L, Rhodes A, Alhazzani W, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign: International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock 2021. Crit Care Med 2021;49(11):e1063–e1143.

items.stem: Select the findings that should raise sepsis in a patient with suspected infection.

options.text: New confusion or any change in mental status
options.rationale: Organ dysfunction, and frequently the first sign in the elderly.

options.text: Raised respiratory rate
options.rationale: Among the earliest and most sensitive findings.

options.text: Tachycardia with warm or flushed skin
options.rationale: Distributive shock that does not look like shock.

options.text: Temperature high or low — hypothermia counts
options.rationale: A low temperature in infection is a bad sign, not a reassuring one.

options.text: A normal blood pressure
options.rationale: It is common early and excludes nothing.

items.explanation_md: Rate, mental status, skin and temperature. None needs equipment, and together they find far more septic patients than any single score.
items.source_ref: Evans L, Rhodes A, Alhazzani W, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign: International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock 2021. Crit Care Med 2021;49(11):e1063–e1143.

items.stem: An 80-year-old is confused and breathing at 26, with warm skin and a temperature of 35.6°C. What should you consider?

options.text: Sepsis — hypothermia, new confusion and a raised respiratory rate together are a classic presentation in the old
options.rationale: No fever, and that makes it more concerning rather than less.

options.text: Sepsis is unlikely without a fever
options.rationale: The absence of fever is exactly what makes this easy to miss.

options.text: Simple dehydration
options.rationale: Possible alongside, and it does not explain the confusion and temperature.

options.text: Nothing acute — this is normal aging
options.rationale: Chapter 9 said it: new confusion is never normal aging.

items.explanation_md: Older patients often present without fever and without a raised white count. The triad here — cold, confused, breathing fast — is the one to have automatic.
items.source_ref: Evans L, Rhodes A, Alhazzani W, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign: International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock 2021. Crit Care Med 2021;49(11):e1063–e1143.

items.stem: What does inflammation normally do?

options.text: Increases blood flow and vessel permeability locally to bring immune cells to the site
options.rationale: The redness, warmth, swelling and pain are that process working.

options.text: Damages tissue for no purpose
options.rationale: It is a repair and defense response.

options.text: Reduces blood flow to the area
options.rationale: It increases it.

options.text: Occurs only in infection
options.rationale: Trauma and burns produce it too.

items.explanation_md: Sepsis is that local process going system-wide: vessels dilate and leak everywhere at once, which is the distributive shock in 8.3.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

items.stem: Why is a septic patient with warm, well-perfused-looking skin still in shock?

options.text: The vessels are dilated and leaking, so the container is too large and too empty despite the warmth
options.rationale: Perfusion at the tissue is failing while the skin looks fine.

options.text: They are not in shock if the skin is warm
options.rationale: This is the misreading distributive shock is built to cause.

options.text: The warmth is caused by good perfusion
options.rationale: It is caused by dilation.

options.text: Only cold skin indicates shock
options.rationale: Cold skin indicates a constricted container, not shock in general.

items.explanation_md: Every other chapter taught cool and pale as the shock skin. This is the one that is warm, and it is the one most often sent home.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

items.stem: Raises sepsis, or argues against it?

rows.label: New confusion in a patient with a cough
A normal blood pressure
Temperature of 35.4°C with suspected infection
Absence of fever in an 84-year-old

items.explanation_md: Two findings raise it. Two are absences that people treat as reassurance, and neither one is.
items.source_ref: Evans L, Rhodes A, Alhazzani W, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign: International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock 2021. Crit Care Med 2021;49(11):e1063–e1143.

items.stem: What matters most about sepsis prehospital?

options.text: Recognizing it early, alerting the receiving hospital, and moving — time to treatment drives outcome
options.rationale: The interventions are theirs; the recognition and the clock are yours.

options.text: Determining the causative organism
options.rationale: Impossible prehospital and not your task.

options.text: Waiting for a lactate before alerting
options.rationale: You are unlikely to have one and it would delay the alert.

options.text: Distinguishing sepsis from septic shock precisely
options.rationale: The distinction matters less than getting them moving.

items.explanation_md: Your contribution is almost entirely recognition and speed. That is why the screening question — and its known blind spots — matters so much at this level.
items.source_ref: Evans L, Rhodes A, Alhazzani W, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign: International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock 2021. Crit Care Med 2021;49(11):e1063–e1143.

items.stem: Your service uses a single sepsis screen. How should you treat a negative result?

options.text: As one piece of information — a negative screen does not exclude sepsis, and the guidelines say so about qSOFA explicitly
options.rationale: Screens with low sensitivity produce false reassurance by design.

options.text: As ruling sepsis out
options.rationale: No prehospital screen has the sensitivity to do that.

options.text: As a reason not to alert the hospital
options.rationale: Clinical suspicion outranks a negative screen.

options.text: As equivalent to a laboratory result
options.rationale: It is not.

items.explanation_md: This is chapter 1 applied to a tool you will be handed: know what it was built for, and know what it misses, before you let it end your thinking.
items.source_ref: Evans L, Rhodes A, Alhazzani W, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign: International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock 2021. Crit Care Med 2021;49(11):e1063–e1143.

items.stem: How should a past medical history change your thinking on a call?

options.text: It shifts the probabilities before you have examined anyone — some conditions become likelier and some presentations less trustworthy
options.rationale: A history is a prior, not a list to transcribe.

options.text: It tells you the current diagnosis
options.rationale: It does not.

options.text: It is only relevant for billing
options.rationale: It is one of the most useful clinical items you collect.

options.text: It should not influence assessment, to avoid bias
options.rationale: Ignoring it is its own error.

items.explanation_md: Diabetes, dialysis, immunosuppression, anticoagulation. Each one changes what is likely and what a normal-looking finding is worth.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

items.stem: Select the histories that should raise your index of suspicion on almost any call.

options.text: Anticoagulation, after any head strike
options.rationale: A minor mechanism becomes a significant one.

options.text: Immunosuppression, with any infection
options.rationale: Sepsis without the usual signs.

options.text: Dialysis, especially a missed session
options.rationale: Fluid overload and potassium disturbance.

options.text: Diabetes, with atypical chest pain or none at all
options.rationale: Silent presentations are more common.

options.text: A family history of arthritis
options.rationale: Rarely changes an acute decision.

items.explanation_md: Four histories that change the meaning of an ordinary finding. Asking for them takes fifteen seconds and reshapes the whole assessment.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

items.stem: An anticoagulated patient has a minor head strike and is neurologically normal. What follows?

options.text: The risk of delayed intracranial bleeding is meaningfully higher, so a normal examination now is less reassuring than usual
options.rationale: Mechanism and examination both understate the risk here.

options.text: A normal examination excludes significant injury
options.rationale: Precisely the assumption that fails in this group.

options.text: Anticoagulation is irrelevant to head injury
options.rationale: It is one of the most relevant histories there is.

options.text: Only warfarin matters, not newer agents
options.rationale: The concern applies broadly.

items.explanation_md: This is the clearest case of history outranking examination. The patient looks well and the clinical question is what happens over the next several hours.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

items.stem: Does this history change what a normal-looking finding is worth?

rows.label: No fever in an immunosuppressed patient with infection
Normal heart rate in a patient on a beta blocker
Normal blood pressure in a patient with treated hypertension
Normal temperature in a healthy adult with a sprained ankle

items.explanation_md: Three histories that make a normal number less informative. That is what "know the patient before you read the monitor" actually means.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

items.stem: How do genetic and environmental risk interact in most common disease?

options.text: Inherited susceptibility plus exposure and behavior over time — rarely one alone
options.rationale: Which is why family history matters and does not determine anything.

options.text: Genetics determines outcome entirely
options.rationale: True for a small number of single-gene conditions only.

options.text: Environment determines outcome entirely
options.rationale: Susceptibility is real.

options.text: Neither has been shown to matter
options.rationale: Both are well established.

items.explanation_md: A family history of early cardiac death in a 46-year-old with chest pain is not a diagnosis. It is a reason to take the presentation more seriously, not less.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

items.stem: Why is a history useful even when the patient cannot tell you what is wrong?

options.text: It narrows what is plausible — the conditions they already have are the likeliest thing to be going wrong
options.rationale: The medication list is frequently the most informative thing in the house.

options.text: It is not useful without a complaint
options.rationale: It is most useful then.

options.text: It only helps the hospital
options.rationale: It shapes your own assessment and destination.

options.text: It replaces examination
options.rationale: It directs it.

items.explanation_md: An unresponsive patient with insulin in the refrigerator and a dialysis line has handed you two hypotheses without saying anything.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

items.stem: What is the risk of letting a known history dominate your assessment?

options.text: Anchoring — attributing new findings to the familiar condition and missing something else
options.rationale: The frequent caller with a new problem is the classic case.

options.text: There is no risk
options.rationale: It is one of the more common reasoning errors in medicine.

options.text: It only affects inexperienced providers
options.rationale: Experience can make it worse, not better.

options.text: It slows the assessment
options.rationale: It usually speeds it up, wrongly.

items.explanation_md: History raises probabilities; it does not settle them. Chapter 1 met this patient from the other side, as the person nobody assessed properly any more.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

items.stem: What is the honest summary of this block?

options.text: A history tells you what is likely and what a normal finding is worth — and it never tells you what is happening now
options.rationale: Both halves matter, and the second is the one people forget.

options.text: A history is definitive
options.rationale: It never is.

options.text: A history should be ignored during assessment
options.rationale: That discards your best prior.

options.text: A history only matters in chronic disease
options.rationale: It matters most in acute presentations.

items.explanation_md: Use it to decide where to look and how much to trust what you find. Then examine the patient in front of you as though you did not know any of it.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

stimulus.text:
1510. A 71-year-old woman, called by her daughter because she is "not herself". She has been in bed for two days with what the family thought was a urinary infection.

She is awake but confused, and her daughter says she was completely lucid on Friday. Respiratory rate 26 with a clear chest and no distress. Radial pulse 112 and full. Blood pressure 104/58. Skin is warm and dry to the touch. Temperature 35.7°C. Blood glucose 8.1 mmol/L.

She takes a beta blocker, a statin, and metformin. She has not passed urine that the daughter knows of since yesterday morning.

Your service uses a single sepsis screening tool. Applied to her, it comes back negative.

items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

items.stem: The screen is negative. What does that establish?

options.text: Very little — a negative screen does not exclude sepsis, and this one has known low sensitivity
options.rationale: Clinical suspicion outranks it, and the guidelines say so explicitly.

options.text: That sepsis can be excluded
options.rationale: No prehospital screen has the sensitivity for that.

options.text: That no alert is needed
options.rationale: The alert follows your suspicion, not the tool.

options.text: That the findings must have another cause
options.rationale: It does not redirect the differential at all.

items.explanation_md: A screen that is specific and insensitive will let sick patients through by design. Knowing that is the difference between using a tool and being used by one.
items.source_ref: Evans L, Rhodes A, Alhazzani W, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign: International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock 2021. Crit Care Med 2021;49(11):e1063–e1143.

items.stem: Which findings raise sepsis here?

options.text: New confusion over about two days, against a lucid baseline
options.rationale: Organ dysfunction, and the daughter has given you the baseline.

options.text: Respiratory rate 26 with a clear chest and no distress
options.rationale: Respiratory compensation for a metabolic acidosis.

options.text: Temperature 35.7°C with a suspected infection
options.rationale: Hypothermia in infection is a bad sign, not a reassuring one.

options.text: Warm, dry skin with a full pulse in a hypotensive-for-her patient
options.rationale: Distributive physiology — the container has dilated.

options.text: A glucose of 8.1
options.rationale: Unremarkable and not the explanation for any of this.

items.explanation_md: Four findings, no equipment beyond a thermometer and a cuff, and a screening tool that missed all of it.
items.source_ref: Evans L, Rhodes A, Alhazzani W, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign: International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock 2021. Crit Care Med 2021;49(11):e1063–e1143.

items.stem: Her pulse is 112 on a beta blocker. What does that add?

options.text: It is more concerning, not less — the drug blunts the rise, so 112 represents a greater stress than it would otherwise
options.rationale: The compensation you can see is happening against resistance.

options.text: It is less concerning, since beta blockers raise heart rate
options.rationale: They lower it.

options.text: It means the beta blocker is not being taken
options.rationale: Possible, and not the first reading.

options.text: Nothing — medications do not affect heart rate here
options.rationale: This one does, directly.

items.explanation_md: 8.4 said the absence of tachycardia in a beta-blocked patient does not exclude shock. The reverse holds too: its presence means more.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

items.stem: Why is she breathing at 26 with a clear chest and no distress?

options.text: Respiratory compensation — she is blowing off acid produced by failing tissue perfusion
options.rationale: The lungs are fine and are being used to correct something else.

options.text: She has pneumonia
options.rationale: Possible as a source, and the clear chest and absent distress point elsewhere for this finding.

options.text: She is anxious
options.rationale: It does not explain the rate with the rest of the picture.

options.text: It is a normal rate for her age
options.rationale: It is well above normal at any adult age.

items.explanation_md: Fast, clear-chested and untroubled by it is a metabolic sign. It is one of the earliest findings in sepsis and one of the most frequently written off.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

items.stem: Which category of shock does this fit, and what stage?

options.text: Distributive, and compensated — warm dilated vessels, a pressure holding at the low end, and organ dysfunction already present
options.rationale: The confusion says compensation is no longer protecting everything.

options.text: Hypovolemic and decompensated
options.rationale: She is not primarily volume-depleted, and her pressure has not collapsed.

options.text: Cardiogenic
options.rationale: Warm, dry and full-pulsed argues against a failing pump.

options.text: Not in shock — the pressure is acceptable
options.rationale: The pressure is the last thing to move, and her brain is already short.

items.explanation_md: Category and stage together tell you what to do: this is a patient who needs fluid, an alert and speed, and who will look worse quickly.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

items.stem: She has not passed urine since yesterday morning. What is that?

options.text: An organ effect — blood is being diverted away from the kidneys, and it supports the perfusion picture
options.rationale: A slow marker, freely available from the family.

options.text: Evidence of a urinary obstruction only
options.rationale: Possible and not the first reading with this presentation.

options.text: Irrelevant prehospital
options.rationale: It is one of the more useful questions on a call like this.

options.text: Expected at her age
options.rationale: It is not.

items.explanation_md: "When did she last pass urine?" costs nothing and is a perfusion question. Here it is a fourth organ agreeing with the other three.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Pathophysiology.

items.stem: What do you do about the hospital?

options.text: Pre-alert on clinical suspicion, and say plainly that the screen was negative and why you are alerting anyway
options.rationale: Time to treatment drives outcome and your contribution is recognition and speed.

options.text: Transport without an alert, since the screen was negative
options.rationale: That hands your judgment to a tool with known low sensitivity.

options.text: Wait for a lactate before alerting
options.rationale: You will not have one, and waiting costs the only thing you control.

options.text: Alert as an undifferentiated confusion call
options.rationale: True and it discards the pattern you have recognized.

items.explanation_md: Saying "the screen was negative and I think this is sepsis" is a more useful handover than either half alone, and it is defensible in both directions.
items.source_ref: Evans L, Rhodes A, Alhazzani W, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign: International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock 2021. Crit Care Med 2021;49(11):e1063–e1143.

items.stem: What did this call actually turn on?

options.text: Four bedside findings interpreted against her baseline and her medications, over a tool that said no
options.rationale: Confusion against a lucid Friday, a rate with a clear chest, a low temperature, and a pulse that meant more on a beta blocker.

options.text: The blood glucose
options.rationale: It was normal and excluded one thing.

options.text: The blood pressure
options.rationale: It was the least informative number on the call.

options.text: The screening tool
options.rationale: The tool was wrong, and knowing why is the point.

items.explanation_md: Everything in this chapter arrives here: the final path, the category, the stage, the compensation, the history, and a screen whose blind spot you already knew about.
items.source_ref: Evans L, Rhodes A, Alhazzani W, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign: International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock 2021. Crit Care Med 2021;49(11):e1063–e1143.
